subsystems.name: Population data layer
subsystems.role: represents people, households and firms as individual agents rather than averages.
parts: tax, court and prison administrative records

subsystems.name: Behavioural model
subsystems.role: decides how each agent responds to a change in the law.

subsystems.name: Legal-institution model
subsystems.role: encodes the law itself as executable rules, including eligibility, penalties and process.
parts: rule engine for statutes and thresholds

subsystems.name: Simulation engine
subsystems.role: runs millions of agents over simulated years and many scenarios.

subsystems.name: Calibration and validation layer
subsystems.role: tests whether the model reproduces outcomes that already happened.

subsystems.name: Audit and interface layer
subsystems.role: makes results inspectable and contestable rather than oracular.

buildSteps.title: Define the question and the outcomes
buildSteps.detail: Decide precisely which legal change is being tested and what counts as success — crime rate, prison population, cost, or distributional effect — before any code is written.

buildSteps.title: Assemble microdata
buildSteps.detail: Link anonymised census, tax, court and corrections records into a representative synthetic population, using privacy-preserving matching and legal agreements.

buildSteps.title: Estimate behavioural responses
buildSteps.detail: Use natural experiments from past law changes — where one jurisdiction changed a rule and a neighbouring one did not — to measure how people actually responded, rather than assuming it.

buildSteps.title: Encode the law as rules
buildSteps.detail: Translate statutes, sentencing guidelines and agency procedures into an executable rule set, then run it on the current law to check it matches the present system.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against history
buildSteps.detail: Tune the model until it reproduces observed outcomes for a period it has never seen. A model that cannot retrodict cannot be trusted to predict.

buildSteps.title: Run counterfactual scenarios
buildSteps.detail: Simulate the proposed change and several plausible alternatives, reporting ranges and tail risks instead of a single headline number.

buildSteps.title: Adversarially test
buildSteps.detail: Have independent teams try to break the model — gaming, feedback loops, missing populations, and the risk that the model encodes past bias.

buildSteps.title: Publish with open assumptions
buildSteps.detail: Release the assumptions, code and uncertainty intervals alongside the result, then monitor the real reform to score the prediction.

prerequisites.tech: Linked administrative microdata at population scale
prerequisites.why: a few countries with national registers can do this; most legal systems have fragmented, incompatible records.
without measured responses to real past reforms, agent behaviour is guesswork and the simulation is only a spreadsheet.
static tax-benefit microsimulation is already routine in many finance and social ministries; the missing part is behavioural feedback.
unlike physics, societies cannot be put in controlled experiments, so behavioural rules remain the weakest link.
simulating individuals requires access to individual-level data, which carries serious legal and ethical constraints.

pathway.milestone: microsimulation models score the budget and distributional effects of proposed tax and benefit changes, and risk scores inform some sentencing and parole decisions
pathway.unlocks: evidence before votes and hearings, on a narrow set of measurable outcomes.

pathway.milestone: agent-based models that add behavioural response and feedback — how enforcement changes reporting, how sentencing changes plea behaviour
pathway.unlocks: tests of reforms whose main effect runs through people changing what they do.

pathway.milestone: sandboxed pilots where a legislature simulates a bill before voting and commits to publishing uncertainty estimates
pathway.unlocks: a formal, auditable role for simulation in lawmaking rather than ad hoc consultancy.

pathway.milestone: a continuously updated digital twin of a justice system, scored against real outcomes every year
pathway.unlocks: ongoing monitoring of whether a law worked — and the ability to correct it early.
